title: Pipeline Performance Analysis
summary: Quantifying a real pipeline's CPI once hazard stalls are counted in, and why clock speed alone never tells the whole story.

slides.markdown:
**CPI (cycles per instruction)** is the pipeline's scorecard: how many clock cycles, on average, it actually takes to complete one instruction once every stall from every hazard is accounted for.

An ideal pipeline aims for CPI = 1 (a new instruction finishes every cycle). Every real pipeline's CPI is higher than 1, and exactly how much higher tells you how much hazards are actually costing a given program.

slides.subTitle: Base CPI plus stall cycles
slides.markdown:
Real CPI splits cleanly into two parts:

**Effective CPI = Base CPI + average stall cycles per instruction**

**Base CPI** is what the pipeline would achieve with zero hazards — 1, for an ideal single-issue pipeline. The **stall term** sums up, per instruction, the expected cost of every hazard type: structural stalls, load-use stalls, and branch-misprediction flushes, each weighted by how often that hazard actually occurs in the program being measured.

slides.subTitle: Computing effective CPI
slides.markdown:
Suppose: base CPI = 1; 20% of instructions are loads, and 30% of those cause a load-use stall costing 1 cycle; 15% of instructions are branches, mispredicted 20% of the time at a 2-cycle flush cost each.

```
load-use stall contribution   = 0.20 * 0.30 * 1  = 0.06
branch misprediction contrib. = 0.15 * 0.20 * 2  = 0.06

effective CPI = 1 + 0.06 + 0.06 = 1.12
```

This pipeline finishes an instruction every 1.12 cycles on average for this workload — a 12% slowdown from ideal, purely from these two hazard sources.

slides.subTitle: The speedup formula
slides.markdown:
Execution time is CPI × clock period × instruction count. To compare pipelined vs non-pipelined execution of the *same* program:

**Speedup = (Non-pipelined CPI × Non-pipelined clock period) / (Pipelined CPI × Pipelined clock period)**

Both CPI *and* clock period can change between the two designs — pipelining typically pushes CPI up slightly from hazards but also shortens the clock period (since each stage does less work), and the net speedup depends on both moving together, not either alone.

slides.subTitle: Deeper pipelines: clock speed vs CPI
slides.markdown:
| | Shallower pipeline | Deeper pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Clock period | Longer (more work per stage) | Shorter (less work per stage, higher potential clock speed) |
| Hazard/misprediction cost | Lower (fewer stages to flush) | Higher (more stages between fetch and resolution) |
| Effective CPI | Closer to ideal | Pulled up more by stalls |

Going deeper raises the clock-speed ceiling but also raises CPI by making every hazard more expensive. Whether a deeper pipeline actually wins depends on whether the clock-speed gain outpaces the CPI hit for real workloads — which is exactly why pipeline depth is a tuned design decision, not a "more is always better" knob.

slides.subTitle: Clock speed alone is misleading
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "CPU A has a higher clock speed than CPU B, so CPU A is faster."

**Why it's wrong:** execution time is **CPI × clock period × instruction count**, not clock period alone. A higher clock speed with a much worse CPI (deeper hazards, worse prediction) can easily lose to a lower clock speed with a far better CPI.

**Correct model:** always compare **CPI and clock speed together** — why raw GHz comparisons across CPU generations are unreliable, and why benchmarks measure real execution time.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: comparing two real designs
slides.subTitle: When a shorter pipeline beats a longer one
slides.markdown:
CPU A: 5 stages, 1.2 GHz clock, effective CPI 1.3. CPU B: 12 stages, 2.0 GHz clock, effective CPI 1.9 (deeper pipeline, worse hazard cost). Same 1 billion instructions:

```
CPU A: time = CPI * clock_period * N
       = 1.3 * (1 / 1.2e9) * 1e9
       = 1.3 * 0.833ns * 1e9 ~= 1.083 seconds

CPU B: time = 1.9 * (1 / 2.0e9) * 1e9
       = 1.9 * 0.5ns * 1e9 ~= 0.95 seconds
```

CPU B wins here despite its worse CPI, because its clock period shrank more than its CPI grew. Flip the branch misprediction rate a little higher, though (say CPI 2.4 instead of 1.9), and CPU B's time becomes 1.2 seconds -- slower than A. This is the whole reason CPI and clock period must be multiplied together, never compared in isolation.

slides.subTitle: CPI and clock period aren't the whole story
slides.markdown:
Execution time has a third factor besides CPI and clock period: **instruction count** — how many instructions the compiled program actually executes, which depends on the ISA and the compiler, not just the microarchitecture.

A CISC-style ISA might execute fewer, denser instructions for the same source program (one instruction does more work); a RISC-style ISA typically executes more, simpler instructions. A compiler targeting the same ISA can also swing instruction count significantly through optimization. Two CPUs can have identical CPI and clock period and still finish the same program at very different speeds if one runs a program compiled to 20% fewer instructions — which is why serious performance comparisons hold the compiled binary constant, not just the hardware.

slides.subTitle: Averaging CPI the wrong way across benchmarks
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To get a CPU's overall CPI across several benchmark programs, just average their individual CPI numbers."

**Why it's wrong:** a plain arithmetic mean of CPI values silently gives every *benchmark* equal weight, regardless of how many instructions each one actually ran. A benchmark that ran 10 million instructions and one that ran 10 billion instructions should not count equally toward the average — the second dominates real execution time by a factor of 1000. The correct approach is a weighted average: total cycles across all benchmarks divided by total instructions across all benchmarks. Reporting the naive unweighted mean is a classic way benchmark summaries mislead — the number can look better or worse than what users actually experience, depending on which small benchmark happens to have an unusually good or bad CPI.
